414.title: Go to a teacher, fuel in hand (1.2)
414.hook: the leaky boats can't cross, so the Mundaka says what to do next: go to a teacher, carrying firewood
414.howItsDone: In many Hindu traditions students approach a teacher with an offering and study in the guru-shishya relationship; Guru Purnima, on the full moon of Ashadha, is a day many set aside to honor their teachers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: rituals are leaky boats, and your line, the boat leaks. Good for the lake, not for the ocean. Did you ask, once, where you were rowing? Day four hundred fourteen.

When you show up at someone's house for the first time, you bring something. Flowers. A dish. A bottle of something. Not because they need it. Because it says: I came on purpose, and I'm not just here to take. In ancient India, when a student went to a teacher, they brought something too. Not money, not a gift for the shelf. Firewood. Sticks for the teacher's sacred fire. The Mundaka has just said the rites can't carry you across. So what can? Its answer is a person, and a bundle of sticks.
screen: `YOU BRING SOMETHING TO THE DOOR.` → `NOT MONEY. FIREWOOD.` → `WHAT CAN CARRY YOU ACROSS?`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, Mundaka 1.2.12. Having looked closely at the worlds won by works, a seeker should come to dispassion. The uncreated isn't won by the made. To know that, let him go, fuel in hand, to a teacher who is learned in the Veda and established in Brahman. Samitpanih: samit, firewood, the sticks for the sacred fire; pani, hand. Fuel in hand. You met this a few days ago, when the six students came to Pippalada samitpanayah, with fuel in their hands. It's the old sign of a real student. What does it say? I'll serve. I'll help keep your fire going. I'm ready to live the life, not just ask the question. And notice the two qualities named for the teacher. Shrotriya: learned in the Veda, someone who has heard and studied. And brahmanishtha: established in Brahman, someone who lives what they know. Both. Knowledge without living it isn't enough. Living without knowledge isn't either. Then the next verse turns to the teacher, and gives them a duty too. To a student who has come properly, whose mind is calm and settled, the wise teacher should teach, truly, the knowledge by which one knows the imperishable. So the student brings fuel. The teacher brings fire. Both owe something. In many Hindu traditions, this relationship, guru and shishya, is still the heart of how the deepest teaching passes on, from teacher to student, voice to ear.
screen: `THE MADE CAN'T WIN THE UNMADE.` · `GO TO A TEACHER, FUEL IN HAND.` · `LEARNED, AND ESTABLISHED IN BRAHMAN.` · `THE TEACHER MUST TEACH, TRULY.` · then, large: `SAMITPANI.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with your teachers. Bring to mind one person who taught you something that mattered. A parent, a coach, an elder, someone in a book, maybe someone who never knew they taught you. Picture them clearly. Then ask: what fuel did I bring them? Or what fuel could I bring someone who's teaching me now? Patience. Attention. Showing up. Let one of those be your bundle of sticks for today. The bell holds the time.
Go to a teacher. The Mundaka's instruction: fuel in hand, to one who is learned in the Veda and established in Brahman, who then must teach truly.
Your line: samitpani. Today, bring some fuel to someone who teaches you, a thank-you, a question asked properly, your full attention. Day four hundred fourteen.

415.title: From the blazing fire, sparks (2.1)
415.hook: the Mundaka's second chapter opens with a bonfire throwing off thousands of sparks, each one made of the same fire
415.tomorrow: the bow, the arrow, the target
415.howItsDone: In many Hindu homes and temples a lamp or flame is waved before the deity in arati, and some teachers use the sparks of Mundaka 2.1.1 to explain how each being shares in the divine.

segments.voice: Yesterday: go to a teacher, and your line, samitpani, fuel in hand. Did you bring some fuel to someone who teaches you? Today, the fire that fuel was for. Day four hundred fifteen.

A bonfire on a cold night. Someone drops another log on, and the fire answers by throwing up a fountain of sparks, hundreds of them, into the dark. Each one glows for a second, drifts, and fades. Each one is small. And each one, while it lasts, is exactly what the fire is: the same heat, the same light, the same color. Nobody watching says, look, a different thing just left the fire. The student has arrived with fuel. The teacher's fire is lit. And the Mundaka's second chapter begins by pointing straight at it.
screen: `A BONFIRE ON A COLD NIGHT.` → `A FOUNTAIN OF SPARKS.` → `EACH ONE IS THE SAME FIRE.`

segments.voice: The chapter opens: this is the truth. As from a blazing fire, sparks of the same form fly out by the thousands, so from the imperishable, dear one, beings of every kind are born, and to it they go back. Three things are packed into that one picture. First, there are many. Thousands of sparks, every kind of being. You, your neighbor, the sparrow outside. Second, they're sarupa, of the same form. A spark isn't a cheap copy of fire. It's fire, small. Third, they go back. Tatra chaivapiyanti: and there they return. The sparks don't fly off into some other place. They rise from the fire and go back into it. Last week the spider spun a web out of itself. This week's picture is warmer. Spider silk is the spider's, but it isn't the spider. A spark is the fire. Then the text describes the source the sparks come from. The person, purusha, is divine and formless. Outside and inside. Unborn. Without breath, without mind, pure. And from that, breath, mind, the senses, space, wind, light, water and the earth that holds everything are born. Then it draws that person as the whole cosmos: fire for a head, the sun and moon for eyes, the directions for ears, the Vedas for speech, the wind for breath, and the earth from his feet. The schools of Vedanta read the spark differently. Some hear identity: the spark is the fire. Others hear kinship: the soul shares the nature of God, and stays itself. Both keep the fire, and the way home.
screen: `THOUSANDS OF SPARKS, ONE FIRE.` · `SARUPA: OF THE SAME FORM.` · `AND THERE THEY RETURN.` · `THE FORMLESS PERSON, INSIDE AND OUT.` · then, large: `VISPHULINGA.`

segments.voice: Two minutes as a spark. Sit, and feel the warmth of your own body: your hands, your chest, your face. Let that warmth be your spark, small, bright, real. Then think of someone you'll see today, and picture their warmth too, a spark of the same fire. Then a stranger. Then a bird, a tree. Many sparks, one fire. Rest in the warmth, without needing to decide what it all is. The bell holds the time.
From the blazing fire. The Mundaka's picture: as thousands of sparks of the same form fly from a fire, so beings come from the imperishable, and return.
Your line: sparks. Today, when someone irritates you, try seeing them as the Mundaka would: a spark of the same form, flying from the same fire. Day four hundred fifteen.

416.title: The bow, the arrow, the target — om is the bow, the self the arrow, Brahman the mark (2.2)
416.hook: the Mundaka turns meditation into archery: om is the bow, the self is the arrow, Brahman is the target
416.tomorrow: the two birds on one tree
416.howItsDone: Many Hindus meditate by chanting om or holding it in the mind, and teachers of meditation often use the Mundaka's bow and arrow to describe how the sound gathers attention toward one point.

segments.voice: Yesterday: from the blazing fire, sparks of the same form. Your line was sparks. Did you see someone who irritated you as a spark of the same fire? Day four hundred sixteen.

Watch an archer just before the release. The whole body goes still. The breath slows, then stops. The eyes stop darting. For one second, there's nothing in the world but the line from the arrowhead to the mark. Archers say that if you're thinking about your dinner, you'll miss. In ancient India, archery was a noble art, and the great epics are full of bowmen. So when the Mundaka wants to describe meditation, it doesn't reach for a cushion or a mountain cave. It hands you a bow.
screen: `THE MOMENT BEFORE THE RELEASE.` → `THINK OF DINNER, AND YOU MISS.` → `THE MUNDAKA HANDS YOU A BOW.`

segments.voice: Two verses do it. The first: take the great weapon of the Upanishad as your bow. Fit to it an arrow sharpened by meditation. Draw it back with a mind absorbed in that, and hit the target, dear one: the imperishable. Then the second verse spells out the picture. Pranavo dhanuh. Om is the bow. Sharo hy atma. The self is the arrow. Brahma tal lakshyam uchyate. Brahman is called the target. Then two instructions. It must be struck by one who isn't careless, apramatta, undistracted. And then: sharavat tanmayo bhavet. Like the arrow, become one with it. Think about what happens when an arrow hits its mark. It doesn't stay separate, hovering an inch away. It goes in. It becomes part of the target. Tanmaya means made of that, full of that, absorbed in it. You've heard maya all week as made of: the self made of food, of breath, of mind. Now the text asks you to become tan-maya, made of that. And om is the bow because it's what sends the arrow. The sound, chanted or held in the mind, gathers attention and launches it. The next verse adds: know the one self alone, in which sky and earth and mind are woven. Let go of other talk. This is the bridge to the deathless. And then a blessing: may you cross safely to the far shore, beyond darkness.
screen: `THE UPANISHAD IS THE BOW.` · `OM THE BOW, THE SELF THE ARROW.` · `BRAHMAN THE TARGET.` · `LIKE THE ARROW, BECOME ONE WITH IT.` · then, large: `TANMAYA.`

segments.voice: Two minutes of archery. Sit tall, like a drawn bow. If you'd like, let a soft om come out on the breath, or simply hear it inside. Let that sound gather your attention, the way a bow gathers its pull. Then let the attention fly to one point: the stillness after the sound. When the mind wanders, and it will, notice it, without blame, and draw the bow again. Undistracted, for one breath at a time. The bell holds the time.
The bow. In the Mundaka, om is the bow, the self is the arrow, Brahman is the target, and the archer becomes one with it, like the arrow in the mark.
Your line: tanmaya, become one with it. Today, choose one task and give it the archer's attention, all of you, until you're made of it. Day four hundred sixteen.

417.title: The two birds on one tree — one eats, one watches (3.1)
417.word: The two birds on one tree
417.hook: two birds share one tree: one pecks at the sweet figs, the other just watches, and the Mundaka says they're both you
417.howItsDone: The two-birds verse is chanted in Vedic recitation and quoted by teachers of every Vedanta school, each of whom explains the relation between the two birds in its own way.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bow, the arrow and the target. Your line was tanmaya: like the arrow, become one with it. Did one task get the archer's full attention? Day four hundred seventeen.

Late at night, you're on your third episode, or your fourth cookie, or scrolling the same feed you just scrolled. And then, for a second, there's another part of you, a little above it all, noticing. Huh. Look at me. That part doesn't scold, exactly. It doesn't even stop you. It just sees. The Mundaka's third chapter opens with a picture of exactly that. It's older than the Upanishad itself. A tree, and two birds sitting in it.
screen: `THE THIRD EPISODE. THE FOURTH COOKIE.` → `A PART OF YOU, NOTICING.` → `A TREE, AND TWO BIRDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse. Dva suparna sayuja sakhaya. Two birds, close companions, always together, cling to the same tree. One of them eats the sweet fig. The other, not eating, looks on. The tree is the body, and the life lived in it. The bird that eats is the self as we usually know it, tasting every fruit, sweet ones and bitter ones, pleasure and pain, hungry for the next. The bird that watches doesn't eat at all. It isn't hungry. It just shines there, looking on. Then the next verse tells the story. On that same tree, the eating bird sinks down, confused, and grieves, feeling helpless. But when it sees the other, the Lord, content, and sees that one's greatness, its grief is gone. Notice: the eating bird doesn't have to fly to another tree. The watcher was on the same branch the whole time. This verse wasn't new when the Mundaka used it. It comes from the Rig Veda, from a hymn of riddles, and the Shvetashvatara Upanishad quotes it too. And here's where the schools of Vedanta part ways, honestly and for centuries. Advaita teachers read the two birds as one self seen two ways: the watcher is who the eater really is. Madhva's Dvaita school reads them as forever two, the soul and God, close companions who never merge. Ramanuja's school reads them as two, inseparably joined, the soul within God as a body within its self. All of them keep the comfort of the verse. The eater isn't alone. The watcher was always there.
screen: `TWO BIRDS, CLOSE COMPANIONS, ONE TREE.` · `ONE EATS THE SWEET FIG.` · `THE OTHER, NOT EATING, LOOKS ON.` · `SEEING THE WATCHER, GRIEF ENDS.` · then, large: `DVA SUPARNA.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with two birds. Sit, and let the eating bird be busy: thoughts, wants, a little itch, a plan for later. Let it peck. Now notice that something sees the pecking. It doesn't eat. It doesn't hurry. Rest with that one for a breath. When you get caught up in the pecking again, that's fine. Just look up, the way the eating bird looked up and saw its companion, still there on the same branch. The bell holds the time.
The two birds on one tree. In the Mundaka, one eats the sweet fruit and grieves; the other looks on, content; and seeing it, the first is freed from grief.
Your line: the one who watches. Today, in the middle of a craving or a scroll, look up, once, at the bird on the same branch. Day four hundred seventeen.

418.title: "Truth alone prevails" — satyam eva jayate (3.1)
418.hook: three words from the Mundaka sit on India's national emblem; most people who carry them in their pockets have never read the verse
418.tomorrow: not by eye, not by speech
418.howItsDone: Satyameva jayate is printed beneath India's national emblem on currency and official documents, and many Hindu schools, families and teachers quote it as a reminder that truthfulness is part of dharma.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the two birds on one tree, and your line, the one who watches. Did you look up, once, at the bird on the same branch? Day four hundred eighteen.

If you've ever held Indian money, you've held this lesson. Look at the national emblem: the lions, back to back, taken from a pillar of the emperor Ashoka. Underneath them, in Devanagari script, three words. Satyameva jayate. Truth alone prevails. They're on India's banknotes and coins, on government seals and documents. Millions of people carry them every day, in wallets and pockets. Far fewer know where the words come from. They come from the Mundaka Upanishad, from the chapter we're reading right now. And the full verse says a good deal more than the emblem has room for.
screen: `THE LIONS OF ASHOKA'S PILLAR.` → `SATYAMEVA JAYATE.` → `FROM THE MUNDAKA UPANISHAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line of the verse: satyam eva jayate, nanritam. Truth alone wins, not untruth. Satya, truth, comes from sat, what is, what's real. So truth here is more than accurate words. It's being in line with what actually is. Eva means only, alone. And nanritam, not anritam: anrita is the crooked, the false, the opposite of rita, the right order of things. So: what is real wins. What's crooked doesn't. Then the verse keeps going, and this is the part the coins leave off. By truth the road is laid out, the path of the gods, on which the sages travel, their desires fulfilled, to the place where truth's highest treasure is. So truth isn't only the winner of an argument. It's a road. You walk on it, and it takes you somewhere. That fits the neighboring verses. Just before this, the Mundaka says the self is reached by truth, by discipline, by right knowledge, by a disciplined life. Truthfulness isn't a rule stuck on the outside of spiritual life. It's the pavement. The words became a national motto when India became a republic, in 1950, and many people credit the independence leader Madan Mohan Malaviya with making them a rallying cry years earlier. It's a hopeful choice for a country's seal. It doesn't claim that truth wins quickly, or every day, or in every courtroom. The Upanishad's claim is longer and quieter. Over the whole road, what is real holds, and what's crooked doesn't.
screen: `TRUTH ALONE WINS, NOT UNTRUTH.` · `SATYA: WHAT IS REAL.` · `BY TRUTH THE ROAD IS LAID.` · `A REPUBLIC'S MOTTO, 1950.` · then, large: `SATYAMEVA JAYATE.`

segments.voice: Two minutes on the road of truth. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then bring to mind one small place in your life where something is a little crooked: a fib you told to keep the peace, a thing you said you'd do and didn't, a story you tell yourself that isn't quite so. No shame. Just look at it plainly. Then picture what it would be like to set that one stone straight. Rest in that picture. The bell holds the time.
Truth alone prevails. Satyam eva jayate, from Mundaka 3.1: truth wins, not untruth, and by truth the road of the gods is laid.
Your line: the motto on the coins. Today, the next time you handle money, let it remind you of three words, and straighten one small crooked thing. Day four hundred eighteen.

419.title: Not by eye, not by speech — by the mind made pure (3.1)
419.hook: the Mundaka lists the ways the self can't be grasped, and then names the one way it can: a mind gone clear
419.tomorrow: the rivers lose their names in the sea
419.howItsDone: Many Hindus understand practices like japa, meditation, fasting and worship as ways of purifying the mind (chitta-shuddhi), so that knowledge can arise, rather than as ends in themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday: truth alone prevails, and your line, the motto on the coins. Did handling money remind you to straighten one small crooked thing? Day four hundred nineteen.

Scoop up a glass of river water after a storm. It's brown, swirling, you can't see a thing through it. Now set it on the counter and leave it alone. You don't filter it. You don't stir it. You just let it be. An hour later, the mud has settled to the bottom, and you can see straight through to the other side. Nothing was added. Something just stopped moving. The Mundaka has been telling us about the self for two chapters. Now it tells us how it's seen, and first, how it isn't.
screen: `A GLASS OF MUDDY RIVER WATER.` → `LEAVE IT ALONE.` → `AN HOUR LATER, CLEAR.`

segments.voice: The verse starts with a list of no. Na chakshusha grihyate: it isn't grasped by the eye. Not by speech either. Not by the other senses. Not by austerity, and not by works. That's a surprising list, because two of those, tapas and ritual works, have been honored all through this Upanishad. You learned the rites were true, and the arrow was sharpened by meditation. But they're not the hand that grasps it. Then comes the yes. Jnana-prasadena vishuddha-sattvah. By the clearness of knowledge, the one whose being is purified, meditating, sees it, the one without parts. Prasada is a lovely word. It means clearness, calm, settling, like water once the mud has sunk. It also means grace and favor; temple food is called prasad for that reason. Here it's knowledge gone clear. And vishuddha-sattva is a being made thoroughly clean. The next verse says how. The self is subtle, and known by thought, by a mind in which the five breaths have entered, and the whole mind of creatures is woven through with the senses. When that mind is purified, the self shines out. So the senses, speech, discipline and ritual aren't thrown away. They're more like the stirring stick and the filter. Useful. But the seeing happens when the water stops moving. That's why the verse ends with meditating. It isn't another technique to add. It's what happens when the mind finally sits still long enough to become clear.
screen: `NOT BY EYE, NOT BY SPEECH.` · `NOT BY AUSTERITY OR WORKS.` · `BY THE CLEARNESS OF KNOWLEDGE.` · `A PURIFIED MIND, AND THE SELF SHINES.` · then, large: `JNANA-PRASADA.`

segments.voice: Two minutes as the glass of water. Sit still, and let whatever is stirred up in you be stirred up: today's conversations, a worry, a song stuck in your head. Don't try to filter it. Don't stir. Just stop adding motion. Notice how, with each breath, some of it sinks a little lower. You don't have to make the water clear. You only have to leave it alone, and look. The bell holds the time.
Not by eye. In the Mundaka, the self isn't grasped by eye, speech, austerity or works, but by the clearness of knowledge, in a mind made pure.
Your line: purified. Today, when your mind gets muddy, stop stirring for one minute and let something settle before you decide anything. Day four hundred nineteen.

420.title: The rivers lose their names in the sea; the knower becomes the Brahman (3.2)
420.word: The rivers lose their names in t
420.hook: the Mundaka ends at the coast: rivers reaching the sea, letting go of their names, and a knower who becomes what they know
420.howItsDone: The Mundaka closes with 'namah parama-rishibhyah' repeated twice, and in traditional recitation students end their study of it the same way; many Hindus also immerse ashes in rivers that flow to the sea.

segments.voice: Yesterday: not by eye, not by speech, but by a mind gone clear. Your line was purified. Did you stop stirring, once, and let something settle? Day four hundred twenty, the end of week sixty.

The Ganga starts in the Himalayas, under a glacier. For more than two thousand kilometers it has a name, a goddess, temples on its banks, cities that live by it. People bathe in it, scatter ashes in it, sing to it. And then it reaches the Bay of Bengal. A few miles out, scoop up a cup of water, and try to say which part is the Ganga. You can't. It hasn't been destroyed. It's arrived. Ten days ago, the Prashna used this picture for the sixteen parts. Today the Mundaka ends with it, and turns it on the one who knows.
screen: `A RIVER WITH A NAME AND A GODDESS.` → `THEN, THE SEA.` → `NOT DESTROYED. ARRIVED.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse. Yatha nadyah syandamanah samudre astam gacchanti nama-rupe vihaya. As rivers flowing on go home into the sea, leaving name and form behind, so the knower, freed from name and form, goes to the divine person, higher than the high. Nama-rupa: name and form. It's the Upanishads' phrase for everything that makes a thing this thing and not that one. The label and the shape. A river is mostly name and form. Water is water. What made it the Ganga was the name, and the banks. Astam gacchanti is a lovely phrase too. It's what the sun does at evening: it goes home, it sets. The rivers don't vanish. They set into the sea. Then the next verse makes the boldest claim in the whole Upanishad. Sa yo ha vai tat paramam brahma veda brahmaiva bhavati. Whoever knows that highest Brahman becomes Brahman itself. That person crosses over grief, crosses over wrongdoing, and, freed from the knots of the heart, becomes immortal. Here, as with the two birds, the schools read differently. Advaita teachers take it plainly: the knower is Brahman, and always was; only name and form fell away. Other Vedanta teachers read becomes Brahman as becoming like Brahman, reaching it, sharing its joy, while the soul stays itself. Both keep the sea. And then the Mundaka closes, after one last instruction about who should be taught, with a bow to its teachers. Namah parama-rishibhyah. Honor to the great seers. Twice.
screen: `RIVERS GO HOME INTO THE SEA.` · `NAMA-RUPA: NAME AND FORM.` · `THE KNOWER OF BRAHMAN BECOMES BRAHMAN.` · `HONOR TO THE GREAT SEERS.` · then, large: `NAMA-RUPE VIHAYA.`

segments.voice: Two minutes of setting your name down. Sit, and quietly say your name to yourself once. Then your roles: a child of someone, a friend, a worker, whatever you are to people. Hold them for a moment. Then, gently, let them sit beside you, like shoes left at a door. You'll pick them up again. For now, notice what's here without the labels: breathing, aware, simply being. Rest in that wide water. The bell holds the time.
The rivers lose their names in the sea. The Mundaka's last picture: as rivers set into the sea, the knower, free of name and form, reaches the highest, and becomes Brahman.
screen: `THE RIVERS AND THE SEA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: nama-rupa gone. Today, meet one person without their label first. And that's week sixty: fuel in hand, sparks, the bow, two birds, truth prevails, purified, and the rivers. Day four hundred twenty.
screen: `WEEK SIXTY: FUEL IN HAND · SPARKS · THE BOW · TWO BIRDS · TRUTH · PURIFIED · THE RIVERS`
